summary:
The Altai Republic stands under the national framework of Russia, and no sub-national deviation from that framework has been identified in the sources; the territory is therefore assessed at the national score. Within the republic, Russia's laws apply in full: legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and same-sex marriage is banned, while same-sex sexual activity itself is not criminalised.

The expanded propaganda statute criminalises public expression that, explicitly, justifies gender transition. Penalties reach administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment.

Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as an extremist organisation, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years under Article 282.2 of the criminal code.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, roughly 98 administrative and three criminal, for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The UK Home Office assesses that openly LGBT+ people in Russia are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, and that the state is able but not willing to provide protection; it records at least 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, do not travel, for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention, active war and arbitrary law enforcement.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement wave documented nationally has no identified regional carve-out for the Altai Republic; the extremism convictions recorded by Human Rights Watch span administrative and criminal courts across the country, and the propaganda-law fine volume reported by Meduza reflects nationwide processing.

Physical coercion against transgender people in Russia is documented independently of the criminal statutes: BBC Russian reported in July 2024 on a transgender woman held for nine months at a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, in Siberia, where she was forced to take testosterone before escaping.

The US advisory's Level 4 rating applies to all travellers and is not specific to LGBT status, so a trans visitor to the Altai Republic faces both the general arbitrary-law-enforcement risk and the trans-specific statutory risk simultaneously.
localsOnly:
Residents of the Altai Republic live under the same 2023 ban on legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care that applies throughout Russia, with no regional exception identified; gender-marker changes on official documents are unavailable locally as elsewhere.

The UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims and is relied on by those seeking to leave.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Altai Republic-specific enforcement data, local court records, or regional police practice regarding LGBT+ or transgender people was present in the source inventory; the assessment rests on the national framework with no identified sub-national deviation, which is an absence of contrary evidence rather than positive confirmation of local conditions.

Whether medical providers in the Altai Republic had previously offered gender-affirming care before the 2023 national ban, and how the ban is administered at republican health facilities, is not sourced.
